spatial-u6b066ca643c269ed94-1.text: 1. Approve the attached Spatial Development Strategy of the Russian Federation for the Period up to 2030 with a Forecast up to 2036 (hereinafter the Strategy).

spatial-u9df5537f54cf3761e0-1.text: 2. The Ministry of Economic Development of Russia shall, within 3 months, submit to the Government of the Russian Federation:

spatial-ub2c2b4417cee9d29f1-1.text: jointly with the interested federal executive bodies, a draft action plan for implementing the Strategy;

spatial-u6c0bb093641ba4804c-1.text: draft regulatory legal acts on the procedure for approval by the Ministry of Economic Development of Russia of draft regulatory legal acts on the provision, from the federal budget to the budgets of constituent entities of the Russian Federation, of subsidies and other interbudgetary transfers intended to co-finance the creation (reconstruction) of infrastructure facilities, taking into account the spatial development priorities of the Russian Federation defined in the Strategy, including priority development directions for the federal districts of the Russian Federation, the Arctic Zone of the Russian Federation, and the Donetsk People’s Republic, the Lugansk People’s Republic, Zaporozhye Oblast and Kherson Oblast.

spatial-udba031c81b48d369bf-1.text: 3. Federal executive bodies responsible for achieving the target indicators for spatial development of the Russian Federation defined in the Strategy shall submit information on progress toward their achievement to the Ministry of Economic Development of Russia annually, by 1 July.

spatial-ua5ba4acc9e04bf2f94-1.text: 4. Federal executive bodies shall, within one month, submit to the Ministry of Economic Development of Russia a list of regulatory legal acts that need to be brought into conformity with the spatial development priorities of the Russian Federation defined in the Strategy, for inclusion in the action plan for implementing the Strategy.

spatial-udc88498a2014c4731d-1.text: 5. Declare repealed the acts of the Government of the Russian Federation listed in the annex.

spatial-ua10d9c0ad1189dd8db-1.text: Chairman of the Government of the Russian Federation | M. Mishustin

spatial-ua5ae527cc94c374dbf-1.text: APPROVED by Executive Order of the Government of the Russian Federation of 28 December 2024 No. 4146-р

spatial-u9a78f8b3c3fb080518-1.text: Spatial Development Strategy of the Russian Federation for the Period up to 2030 with a Forecast up to 2036
spatial-u9a78f8b3c3fb080518-1.locator: Spatial Development Strategy of the Russian Federation for the Period up to 2030 with a Forecast up to 2036

spatial-ucf25e6a81d6cef0e23-1.text: The Spatial Development Strategy of the Russian Federation for the Period up to 2030 with a Forecast up to 2036 (hereinafter the Strategy) has been developed in accordance with the Federal Law “On Strategic Planning in the Russian Federation”, the national development goals of the Russian Federation defined by Presidential Decree of the Russian Federation of 7 May 2024 No. 309 “On the National Development Goals of the Russian Federation for the Period up to 2030 and Looking Ahead to 2036” (hereinafter the national goals), and the Fundamentals of State Policy in the Sphere of Strategic Planning in the Russian Federation, approved by Presidential Decree of the Russian Federation of 8 November 2021 No. 633 “On Approval of the Fundamentals of State Policy in the Sphere of Strategic Planning in the Russian Federation”.

spatial-u3ad40eafb380abae12-1.text: The Strategy is a strategic planning document developed as part of goal-setting on a territorial basis.

spatial-u68c09ed9ed9d49e59f-1.text: The Role of the Strategy in Achieving the National Goals
spatial-u68c09ed9ed9d49e59f-1.locator: The Role of the Strategy in Achieving the National Goals

spatial-u1d6dbfb588e71f718f-1.text: The role of the Strategy in the system of strategic planning documents is determined by the need to achieve the national goals amid established trends, new challenges and opportunities for the spatial development of the Russian Federation, as well as budget constraints and rising costs in the economy.
spatial-u1d6dbfb588e71f718f-1.locator: The Role of the Strategy in Achieving the National Goals

spatial-u34f93a90580af75f2a-1.text: Implementation of the Strategy will help overcome negative spatial development trends, realize new opportunities and formulate responses to new spatial development challenges, thereby contributing to the achievement of the national goals. Taking account of the national goals, target indicators for spatial development of the Russian Federation have been established as set out in Annex No. 1 (hereinafter the spatial development target indicators).
spatial-u34f93a90580af75f2a-1.locator: The Role of the Strategy in Achieving the National Goals

spatial-u5897c2c2f6d908aa16-1.text: The Strategy is intended to involve spatial resources to the fullest extent in achieving the national goals, taking account of the need to use available resources efficiently. The Strategy identifies spatial priorities that make it possible to concentrate resources from budgetary and extrabudgetary sources, including through national projects and state programs, on addressing key development tasks, as well as mechanisms to ensure their efficient use.
spatial-u5897c2c2f6d908aa16-1.locator: The Role of the Strategy in Achieving the National Goals

spatial-uc109a8fa03ec86f601-1.locator: The Role of the Strategy in Achieving the National Goals

spatial-u7a653ecb5d37cf3c86-1.text: a system of anchor settlements that shape the settlement, infrastructure and economic systems of the Russian Federation and ensure the development of their adjacent territories;
spatial-u7a653ecb5d37cf3c86-1.locator: The Role of the Strategy in Achieving the National Goals

spatial-u94c6e9ad7fa144c5b6-1.text: the main development directions for the federal districts of the Russian Federation, the Arctic Zone of the Russian Federation and the new constituent entities of the Russian Federation, as well as geostrategic territories of the Russian Federation, which take account of their specific characteristics and the new challenges and opportunities for their development.
spatial-u94c6e9ad7fa144c5b6-1.locator: The Role of the Strategy in Achieving the National Goals

spatial-u4d2d5a2354c26a920f-1.text: Efficient use of resources will be achieved through implementation of the general and sector-specific spatial development principles enshrined in the Strategy, which provide for:
spatial-u4d2d5a2354c26a920f-1.locator: The Role of the Strategy in Achieving the National Goals

spatial-u3f58cd67046a0b2e92-1.text: ensuring maximum utilization of existing infrastructure facilities;
spatial-u3f58cd67046a0b2e92-1.locator: The Role of the Strategy in Achieving the National Goals

spatial-u6a5a816237c78dec78-1.text: planning the creation of new infrastructure facilities on the basis of their prioritization, taking account of an assessment of socioeconomic effects;
spatial-u6a5a816237c78dec78-1.locator: The Role of the Strategy in Achieving the National Goals

spatial-u88ee8dafbf953b27a1-1.text: creating centers that provide access to education, medical care and cultural services and meet other needs of residents of several constituent entities of the Russian Federation or municipalities.
spatial-u88ee8dafbf953b27a1-1.locator: The Role of the Strategy in Achieving the National Goals

spatial-u9f4961b89dfaf7ee76-1.text: Spatial development priorities in individual sectors must be reflected in the corresponding national projects, state programs of the Russian Federation and other strategic planning documents.
spatial-u9f4961b89dfaf7ee76-1.locator: The Role of the Strategy in Achieving the National Goals

spatial-ub35096dc1f60cb840d-1.text: Spatial development is managed in accordance with the management model for implementing the Strategy, whose key element is planning based on a system of sectoral and spatial priorities and an assessment of the effectiveness of the measures being implemented. The quality and completeness of analysis will be ensured through the creation and development of a digital platform for managing the integrated socioeconomic and spatial development of the Russian Federation (hereinafter the digital platform), which will interlink sectoral and spatial priorities and infrastructure development plans based on territorial planning documents, and monitor territorial development trends using a wide range of statistical and departmental data.
spatial-ub35096dc1f60cb840d-1.locator: The Role of the Strategy in Achieving the National Goals

spatial-uce2fe188935ea0d701-1.text: The concepts used in the Strategy have the following meanings:

spatial-u266a2df4cb236b247b-1.text: “Geostrategic territory of the Russian Federation” means a territory within the boundaries of one or more constituent entities of the Russian Federation (parts of constituent entities of the Russian Federation) that is of substantial importance for ensuring territorial integrity and national security and whose development requires additional resources because of specific living and economic operating conditions;

spatial-ubf51657cfd76457e14-1.text: “Urban agglomeration” means a form of settlement comprising one or more urban agglomeration cores and an adjacent territory containing settlements located within no more than 1.5 hours’ travel time of an urban agglomeration core and linked by intensive economic, including labor, and social connections;

spatial-u22cb1c144097e700fc-1.text: “Unified list of anchor settlements” means a list of anchor settlements determined pursuant to an instruction of the President of the Russian Federation and endorsed by a decision of the Presidium (Headquarters) of the Government Commission for Regional Development in the Russian Federation, used in implementing state policy to concentrate resources on a priority basis, including for the implementation of national projects, state programs, program documents and other instruments providing for financing from the federal budget and the consolidated budgets of constituent entities of the Russian Federation;

spatial-uc31cca509f880d790b-1.text: “Small city” means a city with a population of less than 50 thousand;

spatial-ufb87d0de4ad3f73c36-1.text: “Mineral resource center” means the territory of one or more municipalities and/or a water area within which there is a group of mineral deposits under development or planned for development and prospective areas connected by common existing and planned infrastructure and having a single point for dispatching extracted raw materials or their beneficiated products into the transport system of the Russian Federation;

spatial-u68a399e79b2141a5e3-1.text: “New experimental settlement” means a settlement being created in which new approaches are implemented in demography, housing construction, economic, scientific and technological development and other fields;

spatial-u0384e2b9b0ee1a8373-1.text: “Anchor settlement” means a settlement whose priority development contributes to achieving the national goals and ensuring national security, including by ensuring access to education, medical care and cultural services and meeting other needs of residents of the adjacent territory;

spatial-ucea2afdc8b424ffb0b-1.text: “Adjacent territory” means a territory adjoining the boundaries of an anchor settlement that includes the territory (or part of the territory) of one or more municipalities;

spatial-ubee166878309b84046-1.text: “Take-or-pay principle” means terms of a contract for the supply of goods (performance of work or provision of services) that require the supplier (service provider, contractor) to provide the buyer (customer) with the performance specified in the contract (for example, deliver goods or provide a service) and require the buyer (customer) to pay the amount stipulated in the contract even if the buyer (customer) has not exercised the right to receive that performance;

spatial-ueb9c9bb0b426e7614d-1.text: “Medium-sized city” means a city with a population of 50 thousand to 100 thousand;

spatial-uebc970a4a50815c6d4-1.text: “Urban agglomeration core” means a city with a population of more than 250 thousand (except cities in Moscow Oblast). Urban agglomeration cores also include the cities of Pyatigorsk, Kislovodsk and Yessentuki in Stavropol Krai, each with a population exceeding 100 thousand and located within one hour’s travel time of one another.

spatial-u19fb0a8a96d728f60b-1.text: II. Analysis of Trends and Problems in the Spatial Development of the Russian Federation
spatial-u19fb0a8a96d728f60b-1.locator: II. Analysis of Trends and Problems in the Spatial Development of the Russian Federation

spatial-u6fcb3ef86d82a53fe2-1.text: The trends described in this section also determine the main problems of spatial development of the Russian Federation.
spatial-u6fcb3ef86d82a53fe2-1.locator: II. Analysis of Trends and Problems in the Spatial Development of the Russian Federation

spatial-u2cd3dd9a9aad010998-1.text: Concentration of Economic Growth in a Limited Number of Territories
spatial-u2cd3dd9a9aad010998-1.locator: Concentration of Economic Growth in a Limited Number of Territories

spatial-ufd3c67db6f87090d4d-1.text: Despite sustained growth of the economy of the Russian Federation, economic activity continues to concentrate in a limited number of constituent entities of the Russian Federation. As a result of accelerated economic growth in the 9 constituent entities of the Russian Federation that make the largest contribution to aggregate gross regional product, including the Moscow and Saint Petersburg urban agglomerations, their share of aggregate gross regional product increased from 50.2 percent in 2016 to 53.2 percent in 2022.
spatial-ufd3c67db6f87090d4d-1.locator: Concentration of Economic Growth in a Limited Number of Territories

spatial-ua1ccc392021802b847-1.text: In addition to the capital urban agglomerations, constituent entities of the Russian Federation containing the main mineral resource centers, including the Yamalo-Nenets and Khanty-Mansi Autonomous Okrugs and Krasnoyarsk Krai, make a substantial contribution to the economy. Those constituent entities of the Russian Federation remain leaders in economic growth and centers of innovative development and new technologies, and also generate demand for other constituent entities of the Russian Federation.
spatial-ua1ccc392021802b847-1.locator: Concentration of Economic Growth in a Limited Number of Territories

spatial-u9eecc498cee1bf725f-1.text: Concentration of the Population in Cities and Urban Agglomerations
spatial-u9eecc498cee1bf725f-1.locator: Concentration of the Population in Cities and Urban Agglomerations

spatial-u2f6d72eb329b0986b3-1.text: The population continues to concentrate in relatively large cities and urban agglomerations, while the share of residents of small cities, medium-sized cities and rural areas in the population of the Russian Federation declines.
spatial-u2f6d72eb329b0986b3-1.locator: Concentration of the Population in Cities and Urban Agglomerations

spatial-u12767851d5d5f85193-1.text: This trend is driven by uneven development of social infrastructure and other conditions affecting the standard and quality of the living environment. Large intraregional socioeconomic disparities lead to population outflows from rural settlements and small and medium-sized cities to the administrative centers of constituent entities of the Russian Federation and urban agglomerations.
spatial-u12767851d5d5f85193-1.locator: Concentration of the Population in Cities and Urban Agglomerations

spatial-ud9056e94f24a16ce39-1.text: The total population of cities with more than 500 thousand inhabitants is growing: during 2002–2021 it increased by 20.4 percent, from 40.1 million to 48.2 million. As a result, the share of such cities in the country’s population rose from 27.9 percent in 2002 to 32.8 percent in 2021.
spatial-ud9056e94f24a16ce39-1.locator: Concentration of the Population in Cities and Urban Agglomerations

spatial-u25e041b82b549009f4-1.text: Most of the increase occurred in cities with populations exceeding 1 million. The population of such cities grew from 27.7 million to 35.5 million, and their share in the country’s population from 19.3 to 24.1 percent. Over 20 years, Voronezh, Krasnodar and Krasnoyarsk crossed the 1 million population threshold.
spatial-u25e041b82b549009f4-1.locator: Concentration of the Population in Cities and Urban Agglomerations

spatial-ufe807c5a1efd2465b7-1.text: The population of cities with between 100 thousand and 500 thousand inhabitants is declining slightly: from 2002 to 2021 (excluding the increase attributable to cities of the Republic of Crimea), it fell by 1.9 percent, from 28.7 million to 28.1 million. The share of such cities in the population of the Russian Federation declined from 19.9 to 19.5 percent, and their number from 134 cities in 2002 to 132 cities in 2021.
spatial-ufe807c5a1efd2465b7-1.locator: Concentration of the Population in Cities and Urban Agglomerations

spatial-uba5dfaea1198863db6-1.text: The population of small and medium-sized cities with fewer than 100 thousand inhabitants is declining faster than the Russian average: over 20 years it fell by 7.4 percent (excluding the increase attributable to cities of the Republic of Crimea), from 27.8 million to 25.7 million. The share of small and medium-sized cities in the country’s population is also declining, from 19.3 to 17.8 percent, with the share of small cities falling from 11.6 to 11 percent and that of medium-sized cities from 7.7 to 6.8 percent.
spatial-uba5dfaea1198863db6-1.locator: Concentration of the Population in Cities and Urban Agglomerations

spatial-u68e0a7e6ef54b36597-1.text: The rural population is also declining: over 20 years it fell by 4 percent, from 38.9 million to 37.2 million, or from 26.7 to 25.3 percent of the country’s population. The largest rural population decline is in regions of the Central and Northwestern Federal Districts outside most urban agglomerations: from 2002 to 2021 the number fell by 16.9 percent, from 8.3 million to 6.9 million. Meanwhile, the rural population in the Southern and North Caucasian Federal Districts has been growing steadily, increasing by 15.5 percent over 20 years, from 9.7 million to 11.2 million.
spatial-u68e0a7e6ef54b36597-1.locator: Concentration of the Population in Cities and Urban Agglomerations

spatial-u49e810c6696f2a1847-1.text: A trend toward sustained growth is observed in cities and rural settlements within urban agglomerations, primarily the Moscow and Saint Petersburg urban agglomerations, where population growth is faster in adjacent territories, respectively Moscow and Leningrad Oblasts, partly because of lower real estate prices than in urban agglomeration cores and the development of transport systems, including suburban passenger services.
spatial-u49e810c6696f2a1847-1.locator: Concentration of the Population in Cities and Urban Agglomerations

spatial-uec83cd7bcd9e84d00b-1.text: Changes in Interregional Disparities in Socioeconomic Development
spatial-uec83cd7bcd9e84d00b-1.locator: Changes in Interregional Disparities in Socioeconomic Development

spatial-ue93e25b9c5eb70ca6b-1.text: Implementation of a package of poverty reduction measures has contributed to an overall decline in income inequality: the Gini coefficient (income concentration index) for the Russian Federation fell from 0.411 to 0.405 between 2016 and 2023. Intraregional income inequality also declined in 74 constituent entities of the Russian Federation during that period. At the same time, inequality increased in 2023 compared with 2022.
spatial-ue93e25b9c5eb70ca6b-1.locator: Changes in Interregional Disparities in Socioeconomic Development

spatial-u661b7923b248959d35-1.text: Sustained economic growth is observed in the constituent entities of the Russian Federation. Over 2017–2022, the volume index of aggregate gross regional product of the constituent entities of the Russian Federation reached 112 percent of the 2016 level. The volume index of investment in fixed capital over 2017–2023 was 143.4 percent, with growth rates accelerating markedly compared with 2011–2016, when the index was 105.4 percent. Investment increased in 63 constituent entities of the Russian Federation.
spatial-u661b7923b248959d35-1.locator: Changes in Interregional Disparities in Socioeconomic Development

spatial-u76c62ba9e5815da3bc-1.text: Against the backdrop of this growth, including faster growth in leading regions, interregional disparities in gross regional product per capita are widening, from a factor of 3.7 in 2017 to 4.2 in 2022, and in investment in fixed capital per capita from a factor of 4.1 in 2017 to 4.7 in 2023.
spatial-u76c62ba9e5815da3bc-1.locator: Changes in Interregional Disparities in Socioeconomic Development

spatial-ude093a9523e34e78d4-1.text: Trends toward concentration of economic activity are also evident in industry. In particular, from 2017 to 2023, the gap between the top 10 and bottom 10 constituent entities of the Russian Federation in industrial output widened by a factor of 1.3, and in industrial output per capita by a factor of 1.5. As a result, the share of the top 10 constituent entities of the Russian Federation rose from 53.7 to 56.9 percent, while that of the bottom 10 constituent entities of the Russian Federation fell from 0.32 to 0.25 percent.
spatial-ude093a9523e34e78d4-1.locator: Changes in Interregional Disparities in Socioeconomic Development

spatial-ub4344dee6d0af598c7-1.text: Improvements in budget policy and interbudgetary relations are increasing the fiscal capacity of constituent entities of the Russian Federation. Over 2017–2023, estimated fiscal capacity after allocation of fiscal equalization grants increased in 34 constituent entities of the Russian Federation. In 2023, estimated fiscal capacity exceeded the Russian average in 19 constituent entities of the Russian Federation, compared with only 13 in 2017. Estimated fiscal capacity remains low in constituent entities of the North Caucasian Federal District, the Republic of Crimea and the city of Sevastopol. Estimated fiscal capacity is growing fastest in export-oriented regions, including Murmansk and Irkutsk Oblasts and Krasnoyarsk Krai.
spatial-ub4344dee6d0af598c7-1.locator: Changes in Interregional Disparities in Socioeconomic Development

spatial-u94803d520e60c7033d-1.text: During 2017–2022, interregional disparities in fiscal capacity after allocation of fiscal equalization grants, taking into account financial support from the federal budget in the form of earmarked interbudgetary transfers, narrowed from a factor of 2.6 in 2017 to 2.33 in 2022. By 2023, the disparity had fallen to a factor of 2.11 (disparities in various indicators are assessed using the ratio between the values for the 10 constituent entities of the Russian Federation with the highest value of the indicator and the 10 constituent entities of the Russian Federation with the lowest value of that indicator).
spatial-u94803d520e60c7033d-1.locator: Changes in Interregional Disparities in Socioeconomic Development

spatial-ua9c9e09153b43774d8-1.text: The commissioning of residential buildings is growing steadily, from 544 square meters per 1000 people in 2016 to 755 square meters per 1000 people in 2023. At the same time, substantial interregional disparities persist in this indicator, exceeding a factor of 5 during 2018–2023. The least housing per 1000 people is commissioned in Far Eastern regions, and the most in Leningrad, Moscow and Tyumen Oblasts, which attract migrants.
spatial-ua9c9e09153b43774d8-1.locator: Changes in Interregional Disparities in Socioeconomic Development

spatial-udb83f1ea56502f9dc8-1.text: A decline in the rate of official liquidation of organizations between 2017 and 2023 was recorded in 78 constituent entities of the Russian Federation.
spatial-udb83f1ea56502f9dc8-1.locator: Changes in Interregional Disparities in Socioeconomic Development

spatial-u27c3fb97df60a560e3-1.text: Relatively high rates of official liquidation of organizations persist in constituent entities of the Russian Federation within the Northwestern Federal District, where traditional export sales chains have been disrupted.
spatial-u27c3fb97df60a560e3-1.locator: Changes in Interregional Disparities in Socioeconomic Development

spatial-u9c382135d70b9f2160-1.text: A decline in the organization birth rate between 2017 and 2023 was recorded in 66 constituent entities of the Russian Federation. The largest increase in the organization birth rate occurred in constituent entities of the Russian Federation with sustained population growth.
spatial-u9c382135d70b9f2160-1.locator: Changes in Interregional Disparities in Socioeconomic Development

spatial-uc5bcea28c0dfd18ba7-1.text: Deterioration of the Demographic Situation in Most Constituent Entities of the Russian Federation
spatial-uc5bcea28c0dfd18ba7-1.locator: Deterioration of the Demographic Situation in Most Constituent Entities of the Russian Federation

spatial-u4eb6044ae397a30707-1.text: Declining birth rates and natural population decrease have been recorded in the Russian Federation since 2016. In 2023, natural population decrease was 0.5 million and the total fertility rate was 1.41 births per woman. From 2010 to 2021, the number of women of active reproductive age, from 20 to 29, fell by 39.9 percent. The number of women of reproductive age is projected to continue declining until 2046. Under the medium variant of the demographic forecast of the Federal State Statistics Service, by the beginning of 2030 the country’s population will decrease by 2.9 million compared with the beginning of 2024.
spatial-u4eb6044ae397a30707-1.locator: Deterioration of the Demographic Situation in Most Constituent Entities of the Russian Federation

spatial-u63306a0bb5f2c80420-1.text: The number of constituent entities of the Russian Federation experiencing natural population decrease is growing: it reached 70 in 2023, compared with 46 regions in 2016. The greatest natural population decrease is observed in the Central, Volga and Northwestern Federal Districts. The greatest natural increase is observed in the North Caucasian Federal District.
spatial-u63306a0bb5f2c80420-1.locator: Deterioration of the Demographic Situation in Most Constituent Entities of the Russian Federation

spatial-u33dc789a28a34f59ce-1.text: The number of constituent entities of the Russian Federation with negative net migration is increasing, from 50 in 2011–2016 to 54 in 2017–2022. The greatest relative outflow is observed in the Far Eastern and Siberian Federal Districts and in regions of the European North, namely Murmansk and Arkhangelsk Oblasts and the Komi Republic. At the same time, implementation of state policy measures aimed at ensuring economic growth and improving the population’s quality of life in those territories has slowed the rate of population decline.
spatial-u33dc789a28a34f59ce-1.locator: Deterioration of the Demographic Situation in Most Constituent Entities of the Russian Federation

spatial-u581aef03ae0642bce2-1.text: Declining Inflow of Labor Resources into the Russian Federation Due to Increasing Competition in Global Markets
spatial-u581aef03ae0642bce2-1.locator: Declining Inflow of Labor Resources into the Russian Federation Due to Increasing Competition in Global Markets

spatial-u0689a803bde60855b5-1.text: Global migration flows have grown steadily in recent decades: the number of migrants rose from 175 million in 2000 to 280 million by 2020. The largest increases occurred in Europe and Asia, from 56.9 million and 49.1 million in 2000 to 86.7 million and 85.6 million in 2020, respectively.
spatial-u0689a803bde60855b5-1.locator: Declining Inflow of Labor Resources into the Russian Federation Due to Increasing Competition in Global Markets

spatial-u687a5c8a743187466b-1.text: The Russian Federation ranks 4th in the world by total number of migrants, at 11.6 million, behind only the United States of America, the Federal Republic of Germany and the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. Over the past 20 years, the main sources of migration to the Russian Federation have been countries of the former Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, including the Republic of Uzbekistan, the Republic of Tajikistan, the Kyrgyz Republic, Ukraine, the Republic of Kazakhstan, the Republic of Belarus and the Republic of Azerbaijan.
spatial-u687a5c8a743187466b-1.locator: Declining Inflow of Labor Resources into the Russian Federation Due to Increasing Competition in Global Markets

spatial-u42dc4f4643efa71313-1.text: Amid declining birth rates and population aging in the most economically developed countries, global competition for labor, including highly qualified personnel, is increasing.
spatial-u42dc4f4643efa71313-1.locator: Declining Inflow of Labor Resources into the Russian Federation Due to Increasing Competition in Global Markets

spatial-u7177c908a5f36dd5db-1.text: Under these conditions, external migration to the Russian Federation is declining: in 2016 the net migration rate, reflecting the difference between arrivals and departures, was 27.1 per 10000 people, compared with 13.9 per 10000 people in 2023.
spatial-u7177c908a5f36dd5db-1.locator: Declining Inflow of Labor Resources into the Russian Federation Due to Increasing Competition in Global Markets

spatial-ua9fb72a99cb8ca0640-1.text: During the first half of 2024, 4.7 million foreign citizens registered with the migration authorities, one third fewer than in the same period of 2017, when the figure was 7 million. As of 1 July 2024, 2.9 million foreign citizens were on the migration register in the Russian Federation, including 952.6 thousand citizens of the Republic of Uzbekistan (32.9 percent), 667.2 thousand citizens of the Republic of Tajikistan (22.8 percent), and 334 thousand citizens of the Kyrgyz Republic (11.4 percent). Almost half of foreign citizens were registered in the Moscow (42.3 percent) and Saint Petersburg (6.7 percent) urban agglomerations.
spatial-ua9fb72a99cb8ca0640-1.locator: Declining Inflow of Labor Resources into the Russian Federation Due to Increasing Competition in Global Markets

spatial-u45a0625dcdc71ca66d-1.text: The generally unfavorable demographic situation is increasing the risk of labor shortages, primarily in territories with low labor productivity and substantial population outflows. According to the demographic forecast of the Federal State Statistics Service, the country’s working-age population will reach 87.3 million by 2030, after which it will stop growing. With a working-age population of that size, the labor shortage will exceed 2 million.

spatial-u1f1971891392d532ea-1.text: Against the backdrop of labor shortages, unemployment measured using the methodology of the International Labour Organization has shown a sustained downward trend, falling in particular from 5.5 percent in 2016 to 3.2 percent in 2023. Relatively high unemployment persists only in the North Caucasian Federal District.

spatial-u05866b7eef6207c609-1.text: Risks of labor shortages are unevenly distributed spatially, and prospective employment locations may not coincide with territories where labor is excessively concentrated. Thus, under the Strategy for Socioeconomic Development of the Siberian Federal District up to 2035, 377.6 thousand new jobs will be created in the Siberian Federal District by 2030. Meanwhile, according to the demographic forecast of the Federal State Statistics Service up to 2046, the working-age population in the Siberian Federal District will grow by only 270 thousand by 2030 relative to 2024. This creates a need to attract labor, including from other federal districts of the Russian Federation.

spatial-ua512dcc336aabdf5e0-1.text: Increasing Impact of Scientific and Technological Progress on the Spatial Development of the Russian Federation
spatial-ua512dcc336aabdf5e0-1.locator: Increasing Impact of Scientific and Technological Progress on the Spatial Development of the Russian Federation

spatial-u7fc4d0a73f4e4509fa-1.text: The spatial development of the Russian Federation is influenced by technological progress, including the sharp acceleration of the creation and dissemination of qualitatively new technologies.
spatial-u7fc4d0a73f4e4509fa-1.locator: Increasing Impact of Scientific and Technological Progress on the Spatial Development of the Russian Federation

spatial-u1d92c9bc491889c0be-1.text: Russian science currently serves as the foundation for the sovereign development of the state, creating the necessary prerequisites and conditions for well-founded, balanced and effective solutions to the full range of social, economic, cultural and other tasks facing the Russian Federation and for ensuring the country’s security. Science makes a significant contribution to humanity’s intellectual heritage. The need to support domestic science has increased particularly since 2022, following the introduction of restrictions against the Russian Federation by unfriendly states. The role of constituent entities of the Russian Federation is increasing at the new stage of technological development. At the same time, the following trends persist:
spatial-u1d92c9bc491889c0be-1.locator: Increasing Impact of Scientific and Technological Progress on the Spatial Development of the Russian Federation

spatial-u59eb1770ecbda550fa-1.text: a lack of alignment between scientific and technological development priorities and instruments supporting them at national, regional, sectoral and corporate levels;
spatial-u59eb1770ecbda550fa-1.locator: Increasing Impact of Scientific and Technological Progress on the Spatial Development of the Russian Federation

spatial-u2e0686d9a64131f064-1.text: concentration of scientific, technological and educational potential in a limited number of constituent entities of the Russian Federation.
spatial-u2e0686d9a64131f064-1.locator: Increasing Impact of Scientific and Technological Progress on the Spatial Development of the Russian Federation

spatial-u72f9ffff907111b356-1.text: It remains important to develop industry based on domestic technological solutions and strengthen the country’s own scientific and technological base, including by supporting the use of scientific, technological and educational potential and stimulating technology transfer from science to production.
spatial-u72f9ffff907111b356-1.locator: Increasing Impact of Scientific and Technological Progress on the Spatial Development of the Russian Federation

spatial-u2826db7616b12b5476-1.text: According to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, global greenhouse gas concentrations and air temperatures have been increasing since the 1970s. As of 2020, the global mean near-surface air temperature was 1.1 degrees Celsius above the preindustrial level of 1850–1900.

spatial-ued6156109a64c0c36d-1.text: Since the mid-1970s, the annual mean near-surface air temperature in the Russian Federation has been rising by an average of 0.5 degrees Celsius per 10 years, and by 0.7 degrees Celsius per 10 years in the Arctic Zone of the Russian Federation, at a rate 2.8 times the global rate.

spatial-u6207de25d1b50c8d3c-1.text: Climate change has consequences for human and natural systems and poses risks to security and sustainable development.

spatial-ue656e0e13c6fa44507-1.text: Changes are observed in the agroclimatic characteristics of agricultural crops, increases in the frequency and duration of heat, a decline in the load-bearing capacity of permafrost ground, and other changes in climatic characteristics.

spatial-u382c3a60f1af71cb0a-1.text: Recent decades have seen increases in precipitation, the total annual runoff of Russian rivers, although annual runoff in some major rivers is declining, and associated adverse and hazardous phenomena. According to the Third Assessment Report on Climate Change and Its Consequences in the Russian Federation, more than 142 thousand people underwent evacuation or forced relocation due to natural disasters during 2010–2020.

spatial-uc8e9e268f73a7aa863-1.text: Depending on climate change scenarios, near-surface air temperature in the Russian Federation may rise by 2–3.3 degrees Celsius by mid-century compared with the beginning of the twenty-first century. Annual precipitation totals are also expected to increase by 8–12 percent. The area occupied by near-surface permafrost may shrink by 15–38 percent.

spatial-ucfa2b843e3513e10b0-1.text: Climate change creates conditions for natural processes to have a greater impact on regional socioeconomic development, the settlement system and territorial development through:

spatial-u490227c3b4f0538d40-1.text: expansion of permafrost degradation zones and associated hazardous processes, mainly in the Arctic Zone of the Russian Federation, and the emergence of new hazardous zones due to the degradation of mountain glaciation in the North Caucasus and Altai mountains;

spatial-u5acf14b79451d1d52f-1.text: adverse effects of water in flood zones, especially in the Far Eastern, Siberian and North Caucasian Federal Districts, and intensified desertification and land degradation, especially in the Southern, North Caucasian, Volga and Urals Federal Districts;

spatial-u89590a2498fc8e500f-1.text: greater impacts on public health from prolonged periods of heat and forest fires, and expansion of the range of infectious and parasitic diseases;

spatial-u6ca14e9bbe34dd1c67-1.text: the effects of hazardous and extreme natural phenomena on working-time losses, productivity and the labor market;

spatial-u00e4e57af12dfffb2d-1.text: increased destructive effects of temperature- and moisture-induced deformation on capital construction facilities and infrastructure;

spatial-u9f8d52e63e536fee9a-1.text: coastal destruction resulting from permafrost degradation, increased abrasion processes and wave action;

spatial-u31e5122a5ef6f9bb13-1.text: changes in the migration routes and habitats of aquatic biological resources in marine waters and the exclusive economic zone of the Russian Federation.

spatial-udbfbafd4f7bbdf598c-1.text: Since 2019, the Russian Federation has been developing a climate change adaptation system that includes national, sectoral and regional climate change adaptation plans.

spatial-u6ae5aea8e24f3e4412-1.text: Intensification of the Use of Marine Areas
spatial-u6ae5aea8e24f3e4412-1.locator: Intensification of the Use of Marine Areas

spatial-u9a969a52ef3b7fa733-1.text: Economic activity in marine areas and coastal territories is unevenly concentrated, leading to conflicts between types of marine use and disturbing the balance between marine use and the condition of marine and coastal ecosystems. The uneven distribution of coastal economic activity is particularly pronounced in the northern and Far Eastern territories of the Russian Federation, where mineral extraction is intensifying under difficult hydrometeorological conditions.
spatial-u9a969a52ef3b7fa733-1.locator: Intensification of the Use of Marine Areas

spatial-u88fce85d483099e9d7-1.text: Use of biological resources is also intensifying, as reflected in the development of aquaculture and the transition from coastal fishing to fishing in remote areas of the World Ocean.
spatial-u88fce85d483099e9d7-1.locator: Intensification of the Use of Marine Areas

spatial-ud80ea3973ff1325dcf-1.text: These trends require the introduction of planning mechanisms that synchronize development plans for coastal territories with plans for using adjacent marine space. Most countries sharing a maritime boundary with the Russian Federation, primarily European Union countries, have established marine spatial planning systems that, by imposing restrictions on types of activity within national exclusive economic zones, enable efficient use of marine resources with minimal environmental impact.
spatial-ud80ea3973ff1325dcf-1.locator: Intensification of the Use of Marine Areas

spatial-u8c7ea76b9316d36b18-1.text: III. Analysis of Spatial Development Trends and Plans in Partner Countries and Bordering States of Strategic Importance to the Russian Federation
spatial-u8c7ea76b9316d36b18-1.locator: III. Analysis of Spatial Development Trends and Plans in Partner Countries and Bordering States of Strategic Importance to the Russian Federation

spatial-u4a913c5ca874adbc8f-1.text: The territory of the Russian Federation shares land borders with 16 states, 7 of which are included in the list of foreign states and territories committing unfriendly acts against the Russian Federation and Russian legal entities and individuals, approved by Executive Order of the Government of the Russian Federation of 5 March 2022 No. 430-р. Most of the other bordering states are important trade and geopolitical partners of the Russian Federation.
spatial-u4a913c5ca874adbc8f-1.locator: III. Analysis of Spatial Development Trends and Plans in Partner Countries and Bordering States of Strategic Importance to the Russian Federation

spatial-ufe5649d04c24dc40a7-1.text: Unlawful unilateral restrictive measures by unfriendly states are resulting in a reorientation of economic ties and accelerated cooperation with other states, including the People’s Republic of China, the Republic of Türkiye, the Republic of India, the Islamic Republic of Iran, Mongolia, countries of the Commonwealth of Independent States other than Ukraine, and states of Southeast Asia, the Middle East, North Africa and Latin America.
spatial-ufe5649d04c24dc40a7-1.locator: III. Analysis of Spatial Development Trends and Plans in Partner Countries and Bordering States of Strategic Importance to the Russian Federation

spatial-u9b308df56075850b7a-1.text: Numerous intergovernmental treaties and agreements are in force, covering virtually all areas of cooperation with those countries.
spatial-u9b308df56075850b7a-1.locator: III. Analysis of Spatial Development Trends and Plans in Partner Countries and Bordering States of Strategic Importance to the Russian Federation

spatial-u130140a63aa912c2db-1.text: The main areas of potential interaction and integration with neighboring states that are not classified as unfriendly include:
spatial-u130140a63aa912c2db-1.locator: III. Analysis of Spatial Development Trends and Plans in Partner Countries and Bordering States of Strategic Importance to the Russian Federation

spatial-uf52efc57d73a5268eb-1.text: joint development of cross-border transport infrastructure and removal of barriers to increasing trade, including under the Greater Eurasian Partnership initiative;
spatial-uf52efc57d73a5268eb-1.locator: III. Analysis of Spatial Development Trends and Plans in Partner Countries and Bordering States of Strategic Importance to the Russian Federation

spatial-uc5424639c05df1b233-1.text: development of production cooperation in border areas;
spatial-uc5424639c05df1b233-1.locator: III. Analysis of Spatial Development Trends and Plans in Partner Countries and Bordering States of Strategic Importance to the Russian Federation

spatial-u7fe0ed297a294abdb2-1.locator: III. Analysis of Spatial Development Trends and Plans in Partner Countries and Bordering States of Strategic Importance to the Russian Federation

spatial-u2a92ef1af71a4178cd-1.text: Since 2010, the People’s Republic of China has been the Russian Federation’s main trading partner. In 2023, bilateral trade between the countries increased by 23.1 percent compared with 2022, exceeding 228 billion US dollars.
spatial-u2a92ef1af71a4178cd-1.locator: III. Analysis of Spatial Development Trends and Plans in Partner Countries and Bordering States of Strategic Importance to the Russian Federation

spatial-uffc568fe20e973990f-1.text: In 2023, the physical volume of exports to the Republic of Türkiye increased by 25.2 percent relative to 2021, while exports to the Republic of India increased almost 10-fold.
spatial-uffc568fe20e973990f-1.locator: III. Analysis of Spatial Development Trends and Plans in Partner Countries and Bordering States of Strategic Importance to the Russian Federation

spatial-ue62d27e32256567cda-1.text: A high level of cooperation is maintained with most countries of the Commonwealth of Independent States. The Russian Federation’s largest trade volumes are with the Republic of Belarus, the Republic of Kazakhstan, the Republic of Uzbekistan, the Republic of Armenia, the Republic of Azerbaijan and the Kyrgyz Republic.
spatial-ue62d27e32256567cda-1.locator: III. Analysis of Spatial Development Trends and Plans in Partner Countries and Bordering States of Strategic Importance to the Russian Federation

spatial-ud03f1ad93f1f0b62e5-1.text: The main plans of friendly states affecting the interests of the Russian Federation concern the implementation of international transport corridor projects and infrastructure projects, as well as the expansion of economic cooperation, primarily through increased bilateral trade.
spatial-ud03f1ad93f1f0b62e5-1.locator: III. Analysis of Spatial Development Trends and Plans in Partner Countries and Bordering States of Strategic Importance to the Russian Federation

spatial-u5142d56b4eb72a741c-1.text: The Republic of Azerbaijan and the Islamic Republic of Iran are developing the infrastructure of the North–South International Transport Corridor, which will not only promote growth in the Russian Federation’s trade with those countries but also, in the longer term, create a new alternative trade route with the Republic of India and countries of the Middle East and Southeast Asia. The Republic of Azerbaijan also plans to increase the capacity of checkpoints on the state border with the Russian Federation and develop export infrastructure for transporting oil and gas.
spatial-u5142d56b4eb72a741c-1.locator: III. Analysis of Spatial Development Trends and Plans in Partner Countries and Bordering States of Strategic Importance to the Russian Federation

spatial-u1ac00c19bf49d2d2dc-1.text: The Belt and Road concept promoted by the People’s Republic of China combines the Silk Road Economic Belt and the Twenty-First-Century Maritime Silk Road projects. Implementation of this concept involves creating a network of international routes for rapid delivery of large volumes of Chinese goods abroad and initiating transport, logistics, infrastructure and other projects.
spatial-u1ac00c19bf49d2d2dc-1.locator: III. Analysis of Spatial Development Trends and Plans in Partner Countries and Bordering States of Strategic Importance to the Russian Federation

spatial-uc003301c1eab228990-1.text: In a trilateral format under the Program for Establishing the China–Mongolia–Russia Economic Corridor, work is under way to implement projects in transport, electricity, customs regulation, industry, environmental protection, science and tourism. The parties have identified as a priority a project to modernize the Russian-Mongolian enterprise Ulaanbaatar Railway Joint Stock Company. The three parties are examining the construction of a gas pipeline from the Russian Federation to the People’s Republic of China through Mongolia.
spatial-uc003301c1eab228990-1.locator: III. Analysis of Spatial Development Trends and Plans in Partner Countries and Bordering States of Strategic Importance to the Russian Federation

spatial-ub105f533182f98d668-1.text: Interregional and intraregional transport routes are being developed in territories along the Russian-Chinese state border.
spatial-ub105f533182f98d668-1.locator: III. Analysis of Spatial Development Trends and Plans in Partner Countries and Bordering States of Strategic Importance to the Russian Federation

spatial-uc672858cefc6690bd9-1.text: The Republic of Türkiye and the Republic of India are increasing purchases of Russian energy resources, which will require expansion of Russian logistics infrastructure. Demand for energy resources is also growing in Southeast Asian countries. These factors may affect the utilization of ports in the Azov–Black Sea and Far Eastern basins, respectively, and the routes serving them.
spatial-uc672858cefc6690bd9-1.locator: III. Analysis of Spatial Development Trends and Plans in Partner Countries and Bordering States of Strategic Importance to the Russian Federation

spatial-u547c34e2dc73d71d66-1.text: Economic development trends in neighboring states and prospective partner countries may affect the development of individual sectors, including in border territories of the Russian Federation. To ensure economic growth in border territories, priority support must be given to sectors that enable cooperative links with border areas of neighboring friendly countries.
spatial-u547c34e2dc73d71d66-1.locator: III. Analysis of Spatial Development Trends and Plans in Partner Countries and Bordering States of Strategic Importance to the Russian Federation

spatial-u77f28282213e02bb7e-1.text: The Republic of Belarus is the Russian Federation’s main trading partner among the countries of the Commonwealth of Independent States. In 2023, it accounted for 45 percent of the Russian Federation’s trade with countries of the Commonwealth of Independent States. The key area of bilateral cooperation is deepening integration within the Union State, encompassing all spheres of interaction.
spatial-u77f28282213e02bb7e-1.locator: III. Analysis of Spatial Development Trends and Plans in Partner Countries and Bordering States of Strategic Importance to the Russian Federation

spatial-u9dc408b341723eb9d2-1.text: Comprehensive work is being carried out to implement the Main Directions for Implementing the Provisions of the Treaty on the Establishment of the Union State for 2024–2026, which provide for the development of joint production, protection of technological sovereignty and creation of new industrial capacity to ensure the economic stability of the Union State.
spatial-u9dc408b341723eb9d2-1.locator: III. Analysis of Spatial Development Trends and Plans in Partner Countries and Bordering States of Strategic Importance to the Russian Federation

spatial-ua1d04643802649ff44-1.text: Joint cooperative projects in industry, construction and agriculture are planned in regions of the Russian Federation and the Republic of Belarus.
spatial-ua1d04643802649ff44-1.locator: III. Analysis of Spatial Development Trends and Plans in Partner Countries and Bordering States of Strategic Importance to the Russian Federation

spatial-uc559d2b3315e579006-1.text: In 2023, the border regions of Vitebsk, Gomel and Mogilev Oblasts accounted for 28.5 percent of the country’s gross domestic product. Projects aimed at ensuring technological independence and producing high-value-added products are planned in those regions, including for sale in the markets of Eurasian Economic Union countries.
spatial-uc559d2b3315e579006-1.locator: III. Analysis of Spatial Development Trends and Plans in Partner Countries and Bordering States of Strategic Importance to the Russian Federation

spatial-ud7648bef580bd6c971-1.text: The oblasts of the Republic of Kazakhstan bordering the Russian Federation account for 35.7 percent of the country’s gross domestic product. The regions differ substantially in economic potential: Atyrau Oblast contributes 12.4 percent, whereas North Kazakhstan Oblast contributes 1.8 percent. Cooperation between the Russian Federation and the Republic of Kazakhstan includes joint projects for the extraction and processing of natural gas and chromium ore and the development of deep grain processing.
spatial-ud7648bef580bd6c971-1.locator: III. Analysis of Spatial Development Trends and Plans in Partner Countries and Bordering States of Strategic Importance to the Russian Federation

spatial-ucd785e347a71bbb3d8-1.text: The length of the continuous Russian-Kazakh border, 7.6 thousand kilometers, underpins joint cooperation in developing the North–South International Transport Corridor, including the Belarus–Russia–Kazakhstan–Uzbekistan–Afghanistan–Pakistan route.
spatial-ucd785e347a71bbb3d8-1.locator: III. Analysis of Spatial Development Trends and Plans in Partner Countries and Bordering States of Strategic Importance to the Russian Federation

spatial-u1173d79049aa45d236-1.text: Active cooperation is taking place in environmental protection, including the protection and use of transboundary water bodies, and in responding to emergencies.
spatial-u1173d79049aa45d236-1.locator: III. Analysis of Spatial Development Trends and Plans in Partner Countries and Bordering States of Strategic Importance to the Russian Federation

spatial-ud22d8a02ab6b0b3e60-1.text: The economic regions of the Republic of Azerbaijan sharing a land border with the Russian Federation, such as Guba–Khachmaz and Shaki–Zagatala, account for 1.9 percent and 1.7 percent of the country’s economy, respectively. In recent years, the number of major joint industrial cooperation projects implemented with the Russian Federation in the Republic of Azerbaijan has grown, including the opening of a GAZ Group plant producing commercial and special-purpose vehicles and the establishment of pharmaceutical and winemaking production facilities.
spatial-ud22d8a02ab6b0b3e60-1.locator: III. Analysis of Spatial Development Trends and Plans in Partner Countries and Bordering States of Strategic Importance to the Russian Federation

spatial-u9f000cbec44547f225-1.text: Prospects for deeper Russian-Turkmen cooperation involve possible participation by Russian companies in promising infrastructure projects in Turkmenistan, supplies of energy and transport equipment, modernization of water supply and irrigation systems, and industrial cooperation. Of particular importance to the Russian Federation is development of the eastern route of the North–South International Transport Corridor to deliver freight to Turkmenistan, the Islamic Republic of Iran, the Republic of India, and countries of Central Asia, the Middle East and East Africa, including through the Russia–Caspian Sea–Turkmenistan–Uzbekistan–Kyrgyzstan corridor.
spatial-u9f000cbec44547f225-1.locator: III. Analysis of Spatial Development Trends and Plans in Partner Countries and Bordering States of Strategic Importance to the Russian Federation

spatial-u71bfd3c63b805ec408-1.text: The Russian Federation is a leading trading partner of the Republic of Uzbekistan. Numerous industrial parks involving the Russian Federation are operating or planned in the country, in the city of Jizzakh and in Navoi, Bukhara and Tashkent Oblasts. Russian investment in the Republic of Uzbekistan is mainly in industry, transport and energy.
spatial-u71bfd3c63b805ec408-1.locator: III. Analysis of Spatial Development Trends and Plans in Partner Countries and Bordering States of Strategic Importance to the Russian Federation

spatial-u51f10bd357c97ce558-1.text: In 2023, the border regions of the People’s Republic of China, namely Heilongjiang and Jilin Provinces, the Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region and the Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, contributed 7.3 trillion yuan to the country’s economy, or 5.8 percent of gross domestic product. The country’s border regions have border economic cooperation zones with the Russian Federation in Manzhouli, Suifenhe, Hunchun and Heihe, where enterprises focus on exporting products to the Russian Federation and processing Russian raw materials.
spatial-u51f10bd357c97ce558-1.locator: III. Analysis of Spatial Development Trends and Plans in Partner Countries and Bordering States of Strategic Importance to the Russian Federation

spatial-udf78ec427d7399ad35-1.text: In 28 constituent entities of the Russian Federation, 50 joint Russian-Chinese regional investment projects are being implemented in 18 different economic sectors, with declared investment exceeding 3.8 billion US dollars.
spatial-udf78ec427d7399ad35-1.locator: III. Analysis of Spatial Development Trends and Plans in Partner Countries and Bordering States of Strategic Importance to the Russian Federation

spatial-ube7893d81c04c1adc8-1.text: Joint investment projects in transport and mineral extraction are being implemented in border regions of the Russian Federation and Mongolia. Mongolia’s electricity needs are not met by its own generation and are partly covered by imports from the Russian Federation and the People’s Republic of China.
spatial-ube7893d81c04c1adc8-1.locator: III. Analysis of Spatial Development Trends and Plans in Partner Countries and Bordering States of Strategic Importance to the Russian Federation

spatial-u2718e60e96ffd67f61-1.text: In 2023, Mongolia’s economic growth accelerated to 4.7 percent from 3.8 percent in 2022. There is potential for further expansion of Russian supplies to Mongolia of food and agricultural products, equipment and vehicles, pulp and paper products, chemical and metallurgical products, and natural gas.
spatial-u2718e60e96ffd67f61-1.locator: III. Analysis of Spatial Development Trends and Plans in Partner Countries and Bordering States of Strategic Importance to the Russian Federation

spatial-u76c4440e3964df160f-1.text: The Republic of Türkiye is one of the Russian Federation’s largest trading partners in purchases of energy resources, agricultural products and certain types of metal products, a transit corridor for maritime shipments of Russian products to the Republic of India and North Africa, and a major logistics hub for Russian-European trade. Since 2022, economic growth in the Republic of Türkiye has slowed, from 11.4 percent in 2021 to 4.5 percent in 2023, while inflationary pressure persists; together, these factors may restrain growth in demand for Russian exports.
spatial-u76c4440e3964df160f-1.locator: III. Analysis of Spatial Development Trends and Plans in Partner Countries and Bordering States of Strategic Importance to the Russian Federation

spatial-u58bb124cf38e506e77-1.text: In 2023, the Russian Federation became one of the Republic of India’s three largest trading partners by volume of imported products, behind only the People’s Republic of China. The main product categories for expanding Russian exports are oil, coal and liquefied natural gas. The economy of the Republic of India is growing at consistently high rates, at 7.8 percent in 2023, with growth of more than 7 percent forecast for 2024–2025.
spatial-u58bb124cf38e506e77-1.locator: III. Analysis of Spatial Development Trends and Plans in Partner Countries and Bordering States of Strategic Importance to the Russian Federation

spatial-u2604ef8876137b3fe5-1.text: The Socialist Republic of Viet Nam has one of the highest economic growth rates among Southeast Asian countries. The Socialist Republic of Viet Nam plans to strengthen cooperation with the Russian Federation through existing and new projects in the oil and gas sector, including supplies of oil and liquefied natural gas and processing of the latter. Promising areas include joint projects to build new and modernize existing electricity generation facilities in the Socialist Republic of Viet Nam and the development of agricultural cooperation.
spatial-u2604ef8876137b3fe5-1.locator: III. Analysis of Spatial Development Trends and Plans in Partner Countries and Bordering States of Strategic Importance to the Russian Federation

spatial-u17935835cbe27baf3d-1.text: For Malaysia, the greatest potential for increasing trade with the Russian Federation lies in areas supporting food security, namely supplies of Russian fertilizers and agricultural products, in particular wheat, sunflower oil and meat products.
spatial-u17935835cbe27baf3d-1.locator: III. Analysis of Spatial Development Trends and Plans in Partner Countries and Bordering States of Strategic Importance to the Russian Federation

spatial-u88462df7997b36bac5-1.text: In the Republic of Indonesia, promising niches for expanding economic cooperation with the Russian Federation, in addition to exports of petroleum products and coal, include supplies of Russian agro-industrial products to the Republic of Indonesia, primarily wheat.
spatial-u88462df7997b36bac5-1.locator: III. Analysis of Spatial Development Trends and Plans in Partner Countries and Bordering States of Strategic Importance to the Russian Federation

spatial-u934c92483d76fd5150-1.text: IV. New Challenges and Opportunities for the Spatial Development of the Russian Federation
spatial-u934c92483d76fd5150-1.locator: IV. New Challenges and Opportunities for the Spatial Development of the Russian Federation

spatial-u95e98fb4d1987d75d9-1.text: In addition to the trends described above, the spatial development of the Russian Federation is affected by new challenges related to rising geopolitical tensions, including unlawful unilateral restrictive measures by unfriendly states, climate change, global low-carbon development trends, and the accession to the Russian Federation of the Donetsk People’s Republic, the Lugansk People’s Republic, Zaporozhye Oblast and Kherson Oblast (hereinafter the new constituent entities of the Russian Federation).
spatial-u95e98fb4d1987d75d9-1.locator: IV. New Challenges and Opportunities for the Spatial Development of the Russian Federation

spatial-u32fb5ab9ce84a788a2-1.text: The challenges described in this section determine the main problems of spatial development of the Russian Federation and also open up new opportunities for the country’s development.
spatial-u32fb5ab9ce84a788a2-1.locator: IV. New Challenges and Opportunities for the Spatial Development of the Russian Federation

spatial-u120fde58cb7ac37918-1.text: In 2023, compared with 2021, foreign trade with unfriendly countries decreased substantially, to one third of its previous volume, while trade with other countries increased by 52 percent.

spatial-u5d7dbde834e39cdbad-1.text: By 2030, compared with 2021, the Russian Federation’s foreign trade with unfriendly countries is expected to fall to one sixth of its previous volume, while trade with other countries will grow by a factor of 2.5 and account for more than 90 percent of total foreign trade. East and South Asia and the Middle East will become the Russian Federation’s largest trading-partner regions. Countries of the Eurasian Economic Union and other countries of the Commonwealth of Independent States will continue to hold a significant place in the Russian Federation’s foreign trade. Africa and Southeast Asia will be other regions with a growing share of trade.

spatial-u3366e46f8e1c6b62f9-1.text: Changes in foreign trade directly affect the distribution of freight flows among international transport corridors. Thus, in 2023, the share of the Northwestern Route International Transport Corridor, in which trade with European countries had accounted for a substantial proportion of shipments, fell from 42 to 36 percent of total export-import shipments through the various international transport corridors. The share of the Eastern Route International Transport Corridor, used predominantly for exports to the People’s Republic of China and East Asian countries, increased from 34 to 37 percent. The share of the Azov–Black Sea Route International Transport Corridor also rose, from 23 to 25 percent.

spatial-ud17b9c3c63af6a5d07-1.text: By 2030, compared with 2023, the share of the Eastern Route International Transport Corridor is projected to rise by 2.4 percentage points to 39 percent of all export-import shipments. The share of the Northwestern Route International Transport Corridor will fall by a further 2.9 percentage points to 33 percent, while the volume of freight carried will increase by 5.5 percent.

spatial-u6ccb64c1b2358309f2-1.text: Expansion of exports eastward increases the importance of Siberia and the Far East as centers for the future location of industrial production, making it possible to shorten transport distances and improve the competitiveness of Russian goods in foreign markets. The future location of industrial production in the immediate vicinity of seaports is also becoming increasingly relevant.

spatial-ua12555a40c329799f2-1.text: The North–South International Transport Corridor is developing; by 2030 its share will reach 4 percent of total exports and imports through the various international transport corridors, while the volume of freight carried will grow by a factor of 2 compared with 2023. The share of the Azov–Black Sea Route International Transport Corridor in export-import shipments will fall by 1.1 percentage points despite a 9.7 percent increase in freight volume, because of stronger growth in the Eastern Route International Transport Corridor.

spatial-u04088952c302705d06-1.text: Disruption of established logistics chains and longer transport distances are increasing transport and logistics costs and placing greater demands on trunk transport infrastructure. Under these conditions, improving transport efficiency across the entire transport network becomes a priority for the transport sector.

spatial-u5482177937b08ef580-1.text: Freight traffic density on the Eastern Railway Network is increasing. Other railway routes are used mainly as alternatives for moving freight volumes exceeding the carrying capacity of existing infrastructure in the east of the country.

spatial-ud367d521f584bd602f-1.text: At the same time, the existing carrying and throughput capacities along these routes, both in the Russian Federation and in neighboring countries, are insufficient to accommodate growing trade flows.

spatial-u37f12f79439f2e66d1-1.text: Growth is also projected in the Northern Sea Route’s freight base through exports from resource projects being developed in the near-Arctic zone, primarily to the People’s Republic of China, the Republic of India and Southeast Asian countries.

spatial-uc4156402e2d8cdfb3b-1.text: Growth in maritime transport is constrained by a shortage of large-tonnage vessels, including icebreakers, for shipping along the Northern Sea Route. There is a need to develop container transport in Far Eastern ports and along the Azov–Black Sea route.

spatial-u0752e378170b1a1986-1.text: Expansion of port capacity requires continuous coordination with connecting transport modes involved in the logistics chain, primarily rail. Along the Azov–Black Sea and Caspian routes, there is also scope to develop river approaches to ports as an alternative to rail transport in summer and to export directly using river-sea vessels. This factor requires particular attention to projects for the development of river ports and navigational hydraulic structures, as well as to the development of the shipbuilding industry.

spatial-udb998b9ced1d7ed467-1.text: At the same time, transport infrastructure facilities being commissioned, including those intended to remove the constraints described above, do not always meet economic efficiency requirements and reduce the efficiency of the economy as a whole. In particular, expensive projects to create transport infrastructure for low-margin freight lead to higher tariffs for all freight carriers in the Russian Federation.

spatial-uc5eb658f435c9b447d-1.text: Since 2022, military and political pressure on the Russian Federation from unfriendly countries has intensified. This creates a need to ensure national security, including transport, energy, information and food security. This concerns above all territories bordering unfriendly countries, where socioeconomic development conditions and a quality of life conducive to retaining the population must be ensured.

spatial-ue72428804feae6b3bb-1.text: These risks are most acute for Kaliningrad Oblast, whose connections with the main territory of the Russian Federation have, to a large extent, been possible only by air or sea since 2022. This increases the importance of reducing the dependence of Kaliningrad Oblast’s economy on freight transported from other regions of the country and on imports by increasing the depth of product processing within the region and localizing production.

spatial-u553045c9fe6ee6efaf-1.text: At the same time, the cessation of cooperation with unfriendly countries creates new incentives to develop cooperation with other states.

spatial-u475ac927fb791f24ce-1.text: Restrictions imposed by unfriendly countries are reducing the share of imports and access to foreign technologies. This stimulates the development of a supply-side economy oriented toward the domestic market.

spatial-u6ccd94b7793776ef3a-1.text: Domestic demand, both consumer and investment demand, is becoming the key driver of the economy. Accordingly, in the medium and long term, sectors oriented toward the supply-side economy will receive additional development incentives. These include areas focused on import substitution, development of an investment- and innovation-based economic model, and domestic tourism.

spatial-ua7bed78828ecff903a-1.text: Development of industry based on domestic technological solutions promotes diversification, faster regional economic growth, the establishment of new technological chains and stronger interregional ties.

spatial-u8e98e91aa25d5aa70a-1.text: Under these conditions, economic growth in established industrial regions is also accelerating, primarily through machinery manufacturing and metallurgy, where a strong production base has developed historically.

spatial-ua496a5fc42fc1b7830-1.text: Accession of New Constituent Entities to the Russian Federation
spatial-ua496a5fc42fc1b7830-1.locator: Accession of New Constituent Entities to the Russian Federation

spatial-u292c2815aec7455d16-1.text: The accession of new constituent entities of the Russian Federation creates a need to ensure their integration into the economic and legal space of the Russian Federation and to bring their socioeconomic indicators to levels no lower than the Russian average.
spatial-u292c2815aec7455d16-1.locator: Accession of New Constituent Entities to the Russian Federation

spatial-u8bd8cd735ec8fcf229-1.text: The new constituent entities of the Russian Federation have favorable conditions for agriculture and tourism, substantial industrial potential in machinery manufacturing, metallurgy and energy, and a qualified workforce. The accession of the new constituent entities of the Russian Federation made it possible to create a new transport corridor from Central Russia to Crimea. The Sea of Azov became an internal sea of the Russian Federation, expanding opportunities for its economic use, including fisheries, the socioeconomic development of coastal areas and tourism.
spatial-u8bd8cd735ec8fcf229-1.locator: Accession of New Constituent Entities to the Russian Federation

spatial-uef39ad84eb76b61112-1.text: Challenges and Opportunities Associated with Climate Change
spatial-uef39ad84eb76b61112-1.locator: Challenges and Opportunities Associated with Climate Change

spatial-u495c2325afe75e3a26-1.text: The presence of virtually all types of climate risks across the Russian Federation makes it important to conduct regular inventories of facilities most vulnerable to climate change.
spatial-u495c2325afe75e3a26-1.locator: Challenges and Opportunities Associated with Climate Change

spatial-uc9116cfdbd92c3f1e4-1.text: At the same time, climate change creates the following new opportunities, whose successful realization will contribute to socioeconomic development at the regional level:
spatial-uc9116cfdbd92c3f1e4-1.locator: Challenges and Opportunities Associated with Climate Change

spatial-u4cc0b03416b3abfb0e-1.text: growth in the transit potential of the Northern Sea Route and inland waterways;
spatial-u4cc0b03416b3abfb0e-1.locator: Challenges and Opportunities Associated with Climate Change

spatial-uf536963dde28d21cbb-1.text: increased ecosystem productivity in agriculture and forestry, alongside higher forest fire danger and more frequent adverse agrometeorological phenomena;
spatial-uf536963dde28d21cbb-1.locator: Challenges and Opportunities Associated with Climate Change

spatial-uec1a5456c885a700cc-1.text: a shorter heating season, alongside greater demand for air conditioning in summer.
spatial-uec1a5456c885a700cc-1.locator: Challenges and Opportunities Associated with Climate Change

spatial-u57d7c6a9ca887dc74d-1.text: Various policy and regulatory measures are used to implement international climate agreements, including a technological transition in energy from generation based on hydrocarbon feedstocks to carbon-free energy resources and energy resources with low greenhouse gas emissions (hereinafter the global energy transition).

spatial-ua8316118e96f58439a-1.text: The global energy transition is shaping new trends in the sustainable development of energy and the economy at both global and national levels and creating new challenges for regions exporting hydrocarbon feedstocks and other products with a high carbon footprint. A potential decline in demand for hydrocarbons and other carbon-intensive raw materials creates conditions for new markets to emerge in global energy and the economy.

spatial-u9bf6a3cdb71a416807-1.text: In this context, creating incentives and conditions to redirect flows of capital and labor resources at the regional level toward a supply-side economy with low greenhouse gas emissions becomes a matter of paramount importance.

spatial-u096576ddc71ec69679-1.text: V. The Goal of Spatial Development of the Russian Federation
spatial-u096576ddc71ec69679-1.locator: V. The Goal of Spatial Development of the Russian Federation

spatial-ubeaf7a5be3405059cd-1.text: The goal of spatial development of the Russian Federation is to create a balanced settlement system and territorial organization of the economy of the Russian Federation that will contribute to achieving the national goals and ensuring national security.
spatial-ubeaf7a5be3405059cd-1.locator: V. The Goal of Spatial Development of the Russian Federation

spatial-uee16418bcc952eeed5-1.text: VI. Principles of Spatial Development of the Russian Federation
spatial-uee16418bcc952eeed5-1.locator: VI. Principles of Spatial Development of the Russian Federation

spatial-ud8d3a1685a74ce0218-1.text: The principles of spatial development of the Russian Federation define approaches that must be taken into account when setting and addressing spatial development tasks of the Russian Federation.
spatial-ud8d3a1685a74ce0218-1.locator: VI. Principles of Spatial Development of the Russian Federation

spatial-u4834a930a79dfb4750-1.text: The principles of spatial development of the Russian Federation include:
spatial-u4834a930a79dfb4750-1.locator: VI. Principles of Spatial Development of the Russian Federation

spatial-u37bbe0ccaefba65773-1.text: establishing territorial priorities when preparing strategic planning documents, including sectoral strategic planning documents of the Russian Federation, national projects, state programs of the Russian Federation and state programs of constituent entities of the Russian Federation (hereinafter state programs);
spatial-u37bbe0ccaefba65773-1.locator: VI. Principles of Spatial Development of the Russian Federation

spatial-u3ba9f5354d84871a6f-1.text: a differentiated approach to the development of different territories and settlements, providing for the removal of constraints on economic growth in territories with relatively high levels of socioeconomic development and support for territories with relatively low levels of socioeconomic development. In determining areas of support for territories, account must be taken of the demographic situation, characteristics of the settlement system, economic growth dynamics and the level of scientific and technological development, specific natural conditions, and the number of facilities vulnerable to climate change and their importance for territorial development. Priority is given to the development of geostrategic territories of the Russian Federation listed in Annex No. 2, taking account of the main development directions for the federal districts of the Russian Federation, the Arctic Zone of the Russian Federation and the new constituent entities of the Russian Federation, and the provisions of the relevant state programs developed for those geostrategic territories of the Russian Federation;
spatial-u3ba9f5354d84871a6f-1.locator: VI. Principles of Spatial Development of the Russian Federation

spatial-u027abe66d911bcc8ed-1.text: ensuring infrastructure development based on economic efficiency indicators, providing for decisions to implement projects on the basis of assessments of their socioeconomic effects and prioritization of projects on the basis of those assessments, and creating conditions to change consumers’ economic behavior in order to improve the efficiency of infrastructure development and optimize its use, including by introducing the take-or-pay principle;
spatial-u027abe66d911bcc8ed-1.locator: VI. Principles of Spatial Development of the Russian Federation

spatial-u18a622cc11e2b531ad-1.text: ensuring priority development of social, energy, utilities, transport, information and telecommunications infrastructure, communications facilities and engineering protection for anchor settlements, aimed at improving the quality of the living environment in anchor settlements and ensuring their protection against natural disasters and climate risks;
spatial-u18a622cc11e2b531ad-1.locator: VI. Principles of Spatial Development of the Russian Federation

spatial-u68974172aad3b10563-1.text: providing priority support for measures consistent with the priority development directions of the federal districts of the Russian Federation and the Arctic Zone of the Russian Federation;
spatial-u68974172aad3b10563-1.locator: VI. Principles of Spatial Development of the Russian Federation

spatial-u709c239097400ef7de-1.text: increasing territories’ autonomy in addressing socioeconomic development tasks through growth in own revenues and a balanced policy on interbudgetary relations;
spatial-u709c239097400ef7de-1.locator: VI. Principles of Spatial Development of the Russian Federation

spatial-u6c960d5c6bf4b05a63-1.text: creating a system of administrative-territorial and municipal organization that promotes efficient use of budget funds while preserving access to education, medical care, cultural services and state (municipal) services for all residents;
spatial-u6c960d5c6bf4b05a63-1.locator: VI. Principles of Spatial Development of the Russian Federation

spatial-ub767e89bf5efcb03e7-1.text: ensuring priority for the interests of Russian citizens permanently residing in the Russian Federation when implementing migration policy, and preventing spatial segregation, ethnic enclaves and the marginalization of foreign citizens present in the Russian Federation;
spatial-ub767e89bf5efcb03e7-1.locator: VI. Principles of Spatial Development of the Russian Federation

spatial-u0a0499d1e75a7c6d30-1.text: implementing the country-specific priorities of the Russian Federation’s foreign economic policy, promoting the development of international and foreign economic relations of constituent entities of the Russian Federation, and ensuring effective advancement of national economic interests in the world economic system;
spatial-u0a0499d1e75a7c6d30-1.locator: VI. Principles of Spatial Development of the Russian Federation

spatial-u3b5e633bb60e94d692-1.text: taking account of proposals from residents and businesses when planning the socioeconomic development of territories.
spatial-u3b5e633bb60e94d692-1.locator: VI. Principles of Spatial Development of the Russian Federation

spatial-u0c06b9b6734e78ea0a-1.text: VII. Main Directions and Tasks of Spatial Development of the Russian Federation
spatial-u0c06b9b6734e78ea0a-1.locator: VII. Main Directions and Tasks of Spatial Development of the Russian Federation
